fetched_contents.text: Some common statistical methods for assessing rater agreement in radiological studies Abstract Rater agreement is commonly assessed in radiologic studies concerning image quality. There are several methods of measuring rater agreement. To choose the appropriate method, the researcher needs to consider the scale of the outcome variable and the design of the study. This article provides a brief overview of available methods, focusing on the most practical and commonly used, including intraclass correlation, the Svensson method, variants of the kappa statistic, the agreement coefficient by Gwet (AC1/AC2), and Krippendorff's alpha. Additional methods that are not primarily intended for rater agreement analysis but are applied in some cases are also discussed. Keywords: Statistical methods, observer agreement, observer variation, radiological studies, image quality assessment Background The subjective interpretation of radiologic images and the existence of large variations between and within raters have been documented since the 1940s (1,2). Rater agreement remains an important issue in the analysis of subjective rater data in radiologic studies where the variation between raters may be greater than between images (3). Radiology is the field where rater agreement is most studied because reviewing images is easier than evaluating clinical findings on patients by multiple evaluators or in repeated assessments. Rater agreement has, however, been analyzed, albeit more seldomly, in other clinical areas. Yet, rater agreement or disagreement is rarely included as a bias in scientific studies or reported as a limitation outside radiologic research. There are several methods to measure rater agreement, both between separate raters (inter-rater reliability) and within the same rater in repeated observations (intra-rater reliability). Terminology may differ; terms and synonyms are listed in Table 1. Hayes and Krippendorff (4) compared several statistical methods to evaluate rater reliability, such as percent agreement, Bennett et al.'s score, Scott's π, Cohen's kappa, Fleiss’ kappa, Cronbach's alpha, and Krippendorff's alpha. The authors defined five criteria for the properties of a well-functioning index of reliability (4). In this article, we will discuss some of these methods from a radiological perspective and present additional methods, e.g. intraclass correlation (ICC) (5–7), the agreement coefficient by Gwet (AC1/AC2) (8–10), and the Svensson method (11,12). We will also comment on the suitability of other methods not primarily developed for but commonly used in rater agreement analysis. These include visual grading characteristics (VGC) analysis (13,14), visual grading regression (VGR) (15), consensus scoring (16), percent agreement (4), Pearson correlation (17), and the Bland–Altman plot (17). Synonyms may be individual, subject, object, or case Outcome The measured value to which the statistical method is applied. Synonyms may be a response, a measure, or an assessment. The synonym score applies when the outcome belongs to an ordinal scale; a piece of information, usually a letter or a number that conveys the subjectively perceived image quality Rater The human evaluator who subjectively judges the image quality. Synonyms may be observer, reader, or coder Reliability The overall consistency of a judgment. An assessment instrument is said to have high reliability if it produces similar results under consistent conditions. With a high reliability, there is a high agreement between raters and low variation. Reliability parameters are usually expressed as a dimensionless value between 0 and 1 Validity Describes a test's ability to produce results consistent with other measures of the same characteristic and requires external criteria (19) The issue of rater agreement analysis is complex, and no indicator of agreement is perfect, with different pros and cons. In addition, there is no direct connection between the estimate and the clinical utility, where a certain reported agreement can be sufficient in one setting but not in another. For a more robust assessment, the researcher may report two or more indicators, which should point in the same direction. Basic facts and definitions Validity relates to how well the measurements mirror the population, i.e. whether we have a bias in our measurements or not (19). Agreement refers to how well one set of measurements agrees with another set of measurements of the same item. Reliability is a function of the variability, hence, how consistent the sample measurements are and how well one case can be distinguished from another (18). Beginners see more tooltips, experts see fewer to maintain reading flow. Hover over underlined terms for instant definitions. Every supervised learning system rests on labeled data, and labeled data rests on human judgment. But human judgment is neither infallible nor consistent. Two linguists reading the same sentence may disagree about whether it expresses genuine anger or mild frustration. Two medical text annotators may draw entity boundaries at different places. Two quality raters evaluating an LLM response may have completely different intuitions about what "helpful" means. When we train a model on these annotations or use them as benchmarks, we inherit whatever inconsistencies the annotation process contained. This is not a theoretical concern. Datasets built without systematic agreement checking have been shown to contain systematic disagreements that bias model behavior in surprising ways. A model trained on sentiment data where one annotator was consistently stricter than others will learn to predict a blend of their standards rather than any coherent human judgment. An evaluation benchmark where raters frequently disagree will produce unstable leaderboard rankings that change more with the choice of raters than with the actual capability of the models being tested. Inter-annotator agreement (IAA) provides the statistical machinery to quantify this reliability. It measures how consistently multiple annotators label the same data, correcting for the possibility that they might agree simply by chance. Without this correction, a dataset with 90% positive examples and only two labels might show 82% "agreement" even if annotators are guessing randomly. This chapter explores the mathematics of chance-corrected agreement, from Cohen's foundational kappa for pairs of annotators through Krippendorff's alpha, which generalizes to any number of raters, any measurement scale, and missing data. Along the way, we examine how to handle the disagreements that inevitably arise, when high agreement can actually mislead you, and how to choose the right metric for your annotation task. As we discussed in Part VI: Sequence Labeling, named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging require careful annotation protocols. The metrics we develop here tell us whether those protocols are sufficiently clear to produce reproducible labels. In Part XXVII: Alignment and RLHF, we saw that human preference data drives reward modeling. Before using such data, we must verify that human raters actually agree on what constitutes a "better" response. We'll explore preference-specific evaluation in the next chapter on Preference Evaluation, but the foundations we build here apply universally across all annotation tasks. Consider a simple binary classification task: determining whether a movie review is positive or negative. Two annotators label 100 reviews. They agree on 75 reviews and disagree on 25. Their raw agreement is 75%, which seems respectable. But what if 90 of those reviews are actually positive, a highly imbalanced dataset? If both annotators simply guessed "positive" every time without reading a single review, they would agree on 90 reviews by chance alone. Their 75% observed agreement would actually be below chance expectation, indicating systematic disagreement masked by class imbalance. Raw agreement percentages, often called "percentage of agreement" or PoP_o, fail to tell us anything useful without accounting for how much agreement chance alone would produce. This prevalence problem becomes even more acute in real-world NLP tasks. Named entity recognition datasets often have a high proportion of "O" (outside) tokens compared to entity tokens. If 95% of tokens have no entity label, two annotators who both copy-paste the majority class would agree 90% of the time. A chance-corrected coefficient would expose this false agreement immediately. This explains why kappa coefficients sometimes show paradoxical behavior that we examine later. Understanding this denominator is key to understanding both the power and the limitations of chance-corrected metrics. The logic behind chance-corrected agreement can be thought of as asking: "Given how frequently each annotator uses each label, what agreement would we expect if their decisions were statistically independent?" Published in final edited form as: IEEE Access. 2023 Feb 27;11:21300–21312. doi: 10.1109/access.2023.3249759 Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based medical computer vision algorithm training and evaluations depend on annotations and labeling. However, variability between expert annotators introduces noise in training data that can adversely impact the performance of AI algorithms. This study aims to assess, illustrate and interpret the inter-annotator agreement among multiple expert annotators when segmenting the same lesion(s)/abnormalities on medical images. We propose the use of three metrics for the qualitative and quantitative assessment of inter-annotator agreement: 1) use of a common agreement heatmap and a ranking agreement heatmap; 2) use of the extended Cohen’s kappa and Fleiss’ kappa coefficients for a quantitative evaluation and interpretation of inter-annotator reliability; and 3) use of the Simultaneous Truth and Performance Level Estimation (STAPLE) algorithm, as a parallel step, to generate ground truth for training AI models and compute Intersection over Union (IoU), sensitivity, and specificity to assess the inter-annotator reliability and variability. Experiments are performed on two datasets, namely cervical colposcopy images from 30 patients and chest X-ray images from 336 tuberculosis (TB) patients, to demonstrate the consistency of inter-annotator reliability assessment and the importance of combining different metrics to avoid bias assessment. Keywords: Reliability, agreement, inter-annotator, heatmap, STAPLE, Cohen’s kappa, Fleiss’ kappa I. INTRODUCTION In computational health research, it is typical to collect annotations from several expert annotators to capture the diversity of opinion, mitigate subjective biases, and compensate for factors such as the level of experience, expertise, or fatigue [1], [2], [3], [4]. Therefore, it is necessary to (i) assess the extent of agreement between different annotators, called inter-annotator reliability or inter-annotator agreement, and (ii) develop an appropriate strategy for training reliable segmentation models that reflect the underlying agreement/disagreement between different annotators [5], [6]. A typical situation in which it may be necessary to assess interrater reliability is when multiple experts annotate images for the presence or severity of underlying disease(s). In this case, the judgments from different experts or annotators are with discrete categories, such as “presence” and “absence” of lesions, and qualitative assessments as lesions being “mild,” “moderate,” or “severe.” These categories are mutually exclusive; therefore, each case falls into one of these categories. The kappa statistic [7], [8] is commonly used to evaluate inter-annotator reliability in categorical classification problems [9], [10], [11]. However, it is challenging to assess agreement when multiple experts draw boundaries around regions in images. To the best of our knowledge, there are no systematic studies assessing inter-annotator agreement on segmentation in medical images, which is crucial in evaluating the performance of region segmentation algorithms that may be used for the clinical assessment of various diseases. Modern Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques have accelerated the development of automated systems for detecting diseases in images and quantifying disease progression [1]. Simultaneous Truth and Performance Level Estimation (STAPLE) based methods [12], [13] and label fusion algorithms [14], [15], [16] are commonly used to obtain ground truth labels. Lampert et al. [17] presented an in-depth study to quantify the effects of acquiring ground truth data from multiple annotators using different methods. They concluded that the STAPLE and maximizing a posteriori probability-based method algorithms find a reasonable balance between all annotations when the overall inter-rater segmentation variance is low. The assessment of the inter-annotator agreement is essential for several reasons. First, ensuring that annotators’ annotations are consistent is essential to designing and establishing stable AI algorithms. Second, an agreement is desirable for AI model training and evaluation since high levels of inter-annotator agreement help reduce noise and subjectivity. Third, it helps improve the validity of the annotations. Data with higher inter-annotator reliability indicates good quality and supports reproducible studies. The high inter-annotator agreement supports enhanced clinical decision-making and risk prediction. In this paper, we systematically assess the inter-annotator reliability in two applications: lesion segmentation on cervical images and abnormality segmentation in Chest X-ray (CXR) images. Our work makes the following four main contributions: * We propose two agreement heatmaps to visualize and quantify the inter-annotator reliability, including a common agreement heatmap and a ranking agreement heatmap. To the best of our knowledge, no prior works have studied similar agreement heatmaps, particularly the ranking agreement heatmap, toward evaluating the reliability of inter-annotator agreement. * We extend kappa coefficients, particularly Fleiss’ kappa coefficient, from categorical classification to pixel-wise segmentation, by generating and interpreting the new kappa tables for the image segmentation problem. * We apply the STAPLE algorithm to generate the ground truth and compute Intersection over Union (IoU), sensitivity, and specificity to quantitatively evaluate the inter-annotator reliability and variability and compare the consistency of agreement using different metrics. The IoU, sensitivity, and specificity values facilitate the identification of raters with little or high agreement. * We publish a new collection of annotations for the Shenzhen dataset. ## Factors that can affect agreement scores

Agreement scores are heavily influenced by the design and execution of the annotation process itself. The evidence consistently points to **annotation guidelines and instructions** as a primary determinant: poor or ambiguous instructions can create systematic disagreement, while clear guidelines can reduce unnecessary variation and improve consistency. For example, the search material states that IAA is used to validate and improve annotation schemes and guidelines, and that low agreement often indicates unclear guidelines, task ambiguity, or expertise mismatches rather than annotator error [N3-R2][N3-R3]. This means that strong, task-specific instructions are not merely helpful—they are often necessary to obtain a meaningful agreement score.

### How annotation guidelines and instructions shape agreement
Guidelines define what counts as correct and how to resolve boundary cases. When guidelines are vague, annotators may interpret them differently, leading to lower agreement even among careful annotators. The evidence also notes that IAA can reveal task ambiguity, underspecified guidelines, or variation in rater preferences [N3-R1]. This suggests that agreement scores should be viewed as diagnostic tools for guideline quality rather than as standalone quality metrics. In practical terms, a high score with weak guidelines may mask confusion or inconsistent application, while a lower score with well-specified guidelines may indicate a genuinely challenging task.

### How task ambiguity and complexity affect score magnitude
Task ambiguity is another major factor. The same search material notes that low agreement can arise from task ambiguity and that IAA is used to identify ambiguities or difficulties in the task [N3-R2][N3-R3]. This is especially important in complex annotation tasks where boundaries are subjective or the task requires judgment. For example, medical image segmentation studies emphasize that inter-annotator agreement is needed when experts draw boundaries around regions in images, and that variability among experts introduces noise into training data [N5-F3]. In such cases, ambiguity may reduce agreement because there is no single objectively correct answer, and experts may reasonably disagree on where to place boundaries.

Task complexity also matters because more complex tasks can create more opportunities for disagreement. The evidence on medical image segmentation further explains that agreement is important when multiple experts annotate images for the presence or severity of underlying disease(s), with discrete categories such as “presence” and “absence” or qualitative assessments such as “mild,” “moderate,” or “severe” [N5-F3]. In these settings, agreement is not just about binary correctness; it also reflects whether annotators can consistently interpret the same evidence across different examples. The more subjective or context-dependent the task, the more likely agreement scores will be lower, even if the task itself is well designed.

### How annotator characteristics and training influence scores
Annotator characteristics and training can also shape agreement scores. The evidence on medical image segmentation highlights that inter-annotator reliability is assessed across expert annotators and that the study explicitly considers factors such as the level of experience, expertise, or fatigue [N5-F3]. This suggests that agreement is not purely a property of the task; it depends on who is doing the annotation. Less experienced or fatigued annotators may produce less consistent output, while well-trained annotators may be more aligned with each other.

In addition, training and calibration can mitigate differences. The evidence on IAA reporting notes that the goal of IAA is to quantify the degree to which multiple annotators, given the same task and guidelines, produce consistent outputs [N5-R4]. This implies that even when guidelines are good, annotators who are not adequately trained may still disagree more than necessary. Practical reporting considerations therefore include evaluating whether annotators were trained sufficiently and whether training effects are accounted for in the study design.

Overall, agreement scores are shaped by a combination of **guideline quality, task ambiguity or difficulty, and annotator expertise/training**. The evidence supports interpreting low agreement as a sign of problems in the annotation process rather than simply annotator error, and high agreement as evidence that the task, guidelines, and annotators are aligned [N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-F3].

## How to interpret and report agreement scores

Interpreting agreement scores requires caution because a number alone does not fully capture the reliability or validity of the annotation process. The evidence emphasizes that IAA should be reported alongside additional reliability or consistency measures, and that confidence intervals and chance agreement are essential for a more robust interpretation [N4-R3][N5-R4][N5-F3].

### What score values mean in practice and how to avoid over- or under-interpretation
Score values should be interpreted in context, not as absolute indicators of quality. The evidence on inter-rater reliability states that the kappa statistic is frequently used to test interrater reliability and that rater reliability represents the extent to which raters agree [N4-R1]. However, it also warns that different agreement measures have different properties and that no indicator is perfect [N1-F1]. Similarly, the evidence on IAA metrics and implementation explains that raw agreement percentages can be misleading without accounting for chance agreement [N1-F2]. For example, a high observed agreement can be driven by class imbalance or by a majority class, not by genuine consistency [N1-F2].

A useful practical takeaway is that high agreement may be meaningful only if the task and guidelines are clear and the score is adjusted for chance. The evidence on medical image segmentation also notes that agreement is important when multiple experts annotate images for the presence or severity of disease, and that high inter-annotator agreement supports enhanced clinical decision-making and risk prediction [N5-F3]. In contrast, a high score on an ambiguous or highly imbalanced task may be misleading because it does not reflect meaningful reliability.

### How to account for chance agreement and confidence intervals
Chance agreement is a central correction in IAA metrics. The evidence on IAA metrics and implementation explains that chance-corrected agreement metrics, such as Cohen’s kappa, are designed to correct for the possibility that annotators might agree simply by chance [N1-F2]. It further explains that raw agreement percentages fail to tell us anything useful without accounting for how much agreement chance alone would produce [N1-F2]. In practice, this means that reporting only the raw percentage is insufficient; the corrected metric is what matters.

Confidence intervals are also important because they provide a clearer sense of how stable and reliable the estimate is [N4-R3]. The evidence on confidence intervals in inter-rater reliability states that confidence intervals for both measures provided a coverage probability close to the theoretical one [N4-R4]. This supports the reporting of confidence intervals as a standard practice to avoid over-interpretation. The evidence also notes that p-values can indicate significance, but confidence intervals offer a clearer sense of stability [N4-R3]. In other words, a statistically significant p-value does not by itself prove meaningful agreement; the confidence interval tells us how precise the estimate is.

### When and how to report additional reliability or consistency measures
Additional reliability or consistency measures are important because a single metric may not capture the full picture. The evidence on common statistical methods for assessing rater agreement in radiological studies recommends reporting two or more indicators that should point in the same direction [N1-F1]. It also lists several methods, including intraclass correlation, variants of the kappa statistic, the agreement coefficient by Gwet, and Krippendorff’s alpha, and notes that other methods such as VGC analysis, VGR, consensus scoring, percent agreement, Pearson correlation, and the Bland–Altman plot may also be relevant depending on the study design [N1-F1].

In practice, this means that a report should not rely on one metric alone. For example, the evidence on medical image segmentation reports both Cohen’s Kappa and F1-score to evaluate IAA, while also using heatmaps and STAPLE for visualization and quantitative interpretation [N5-F3]. This combination helps avoid bias and provides a richer picture of reliability. The evidence also emphasizes that reporting two or more indicators can strengthen the interpretation of agreement [N1-F1].

Overall, the best interpretation of agreement scores is one that is cautious, context-sensitive, and supported by confidence intervals and complementary reliability measures. The evidence supports avoiding over-interpretation by recognizing the limitations of raw agreement and the importance of chance correction, while avoiding under-interpretation by reporting confidence intervals and additional reliability indicators [N4-R3][N4-R4][N1-F1][N5-F3].

## How agreement is measured in different annotation tasks

Agreement is measured differently depending on the task type because the nature of the annotations determines which metric is appropriate. The evidence shows that categorical, ordinal, and continuous annotations each change the choice of metric, and that task-specific implementation details matter in practice.

### Which agreement metrics are commonly used for each task type
The evidence repeatedly identifies **Cohen’s kappa**, **Fleiss’ kappa**, and **Krippendorff’s alpha** as the main agreement metrics, with some context for continuous or more complex annotations [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]. 

- **Cohen’s kappa** is most commonly used for **categorical labeling** involving two raters [N1-F1][N1-F2]. It is designed for binary or multi-class categorical data and accounts for chance agreement.
- **Fleiss’ kappa** is used when there are **multiple raters** and the outcome is categorical [N1-F1][N5-F3]. It generalizes Cohen’s kappa to more than two raters and is appropriate for tasks where multiple annotators label the same item independently.
- **Krippendorff’s alpha** is used when the task involves **any number of raters** and **any measurement scale**, including nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio data [N1-R2][N1-F2]. The evidence explicitly states that it generalizes to any number of raters, any measurement scale, and missing data [N1-F2].

The evidence also indicates that **Krippendorff’s alpha** is especially useful when annotations are incomplete or complex [N1-R4]. This makes it a strong default choice for tasks with missing data or heterogeneous annotation formats.

### How categorical vs ordinal vs continuous annotations change the metric choice
The evidence explicitly links the measurement scale to the choice of metric. For categorical data, **Cohen’s kappa**, **Fleiss’ kappa**, and **Krippendorff’s alpha** are all appropriate, but they differ in whether they assume a fixed number of raters or more general settings [N1-F1][N1-F2]. For example, the evidence explains that Krippendorff’s alpha can handle any measurement scale, while Cohen’s kappa is specifically for exactly two raters with categorical data [N1-F2].

For **ordinal annotations**, the evidence on common statistical methods for assessing rater agreement notes that several methods are used, including variants of the kappa statistic, the agreement coefficient by Gwet, and Krippendorff’s alpha [N1-F1]. This implies that ordinal labels are compatible with these metrics, but the choice may depend on the study design and whether the scale is treated as nominal, ordinal, or continuous.

For **continuous annotations**, the evidence is less direct, but it does suggest that more nuanced measures are needed. The evidence on medical image segmentation reports both Cohen’s Kappa and F1-score to evaluate IAA and also uses heatmaps and STAPLE to quantify and visualize agreement [N5-F3]. It also notes that the task can involve qualitative assessments, such as severity, which are mutually exclusive categories, and that segmentation tasks require careful adaptation of the metric [N5-F3]. In general, the evidence supports the idea that continuous or spatial annotations may require specialized implementations or complementary measures beyond simple categorical kappa.

### Examples of task-specific implementation details
The evidence provides several concrete examples of how implementation varies by task:

1. **NER and spans**: The evidence on proper ways to calculate inter-annotator agreement for spans/NER suggests that one should consider overlap, exact span matching, and whether annotators have different numbers of annotations [N6-R1]. It also notes that in NER, annotators highlight spans corresponding to entities, and that the task may require a unified and holistic method for agreement measurement [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence further says that F1-score is used alongside Cohen’s Kappa in some settings because it directly reflects overlap between annotated spans [N6-R4]. This shows that span-level NER requires not only a metric but also careful handling of partial overlap and annotation discrepancy.

2. **Segmentation**: The evidence on medical image segmentation reports heatmaps, extended Cohen’s kappa, Fleiss’ kappa, and STAPLE [N5-F3]. It also mentions that agreement heatmaps and ranking heatmaps are used to visualize and quantify reliability, and that IoU, sensitivity, and specificity are computed alongside the kappa-based metrics [N5-F3]. This is a clear example of task-specific implementation: segmentation requires spatial overlap measures in addition to traditional agreement coefficients.

3. **Task agreement in structured annotation**: The evidence on Label Studio Enterprise says that task agreement can be measured with different metrics depending on the task, and that task agreement is also known as “labeling agreement” [N6-R5]. This implies that structured annotation systems often use task-specific metrics and allow the user to choose the most appropriate one for the labeling scheme.

4. **Part-of-speech tagging**: The evidence on POS tagging shows that models sensitive to inter-annotator agreement can perform better on downstream tasks like chunking [N2-R1]. This indicates that agreement is not just a measurement issue but also a design issue: the choice of annotation protocol and metric can affect downstream performance.

Overall, the evidence shows that agreement is measured in different ways across tasks: categorical tasks use kappa family metrics, ordinal tasks can use variants of these metrics or Gwet’s coefficient, and continuous or spatial tasks may require additional overlap or visualization measures [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Task-specific implementation details include handling spans, exact matching, partial overlap, heatmaps, STAPLE, and F1-score [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4][N5-F3].

## Evidence-based guidance on reporting IAA and selecting the right metric

Reporting inter-annotator agreement requires judgment about what is meaningful, how to handle incomplete data, and how to best express uncertainty. The evidence supports a careful, multi-metric approach rather than relying on a single number.

### When a higher score is meaningful versus when it is not
A higher score can be meaningful when it reflects genuine consistency in labeling, especially if the task is well-specified, the guidelines are clear, and the annotators are trained. However, the evidence warns that raw agreement percentages can be misleading and that high agreement may not always indicate meaningful reliability [N1-F2]. For example, a high observed agreement can be driven by class imbalance or by a majority class rather than by genuine consistency [N1-F2]. Similarly, the evidence on medical image segmentation notes that high inter-annotator agreement supports enhanced clinical decision-making and risk prediction, but also that agreement is important because variability among experts introduces noise into training data [N5-F3]. So the meaning of a higher score depends on context: it is meaningful when it reflects true reliability rather than chance, imbalance, or overly simplistic labeling.

A useful rule of thumb is that a score alone is not enough. The evidence on common statistical methods for assessing rater agreement recommends reporting two or more indicators that should point in the same direction [N1-F1]. This helps avoid over-interpretation of a single number.

### How to report missing data or incomplete annotations
Missing data is an important practical issue. The evidence on Krippendorff’s alpha explicitly states that it can handle missing data [N1-R4], which is a major advantage for real-world annotation studies. The evidence also notes that in NER and span-based tasks, annotators may have different numbers of annotations, and that this matters for the choice of agreement calculation [N6-R1][N6-R3]. In such cases, the reporting should explicitly state how missing or incomplete annotations were handled and whether the metric is robust to that.

The evidence on medical image segmentation also provides a practical example: it reports both Cohen’s Kappa and F1-score, and uses heatmaps and STAPLE to visualize and quantify reliability [N5-F3]. This suggests that when annotations are incomplete, it is useful to combine multiple measures and to use visualization tools to show where agreement is strongest or weakest.

### Best practices for reporting confidence intervals and uncertainty
Confidence intervals are central to reporting IAA because they show how stable the estimate is. The evidence on inter-rater reliability states that confidence intervals can indicate significance and that they offer a clearer sense of how stable and reliable the estimate is [N4-R3]. The evidence on confidence intervals in inter-rater reliability also reports confidence intervals for both measures and notes that they provided coverage probability close to the theoretical one [N4-R4]. This supports the practice of reporting confidence intervals as a standard part of IAA reporting.

In addition to confidence intervals, the evidence supports reporting complementary reliability or consistency measures. The evidence on common statistical methods for assessing rater agreement recommends reporting two or more indicators that should point in the same direction [N1-F1]. It also notes that other methods such as intraclass correlation, variants of the kappa statistic, the agreement coefficient by Gwet, and Krippendorff’s alpha may be relevant, depending on the study design [N1-F1]. This means that confidence intervals alone are not sufficient; the report should also include additional measures and contextual interpretation.

### Overall reporting guidance
The best evidence-based guidance is to report agreement scores alongside confidence intervals, complementary reliability measures, and a clear explanation of the task, guidelines, and any missing data [N1-F1][N4-R3][N4-R4][N5-F3][N6-R4]. The evidence also supports using Krippendorff’s alpha when the task involves any number of raters, any measurement scale, or missing data [N1-R4][N1-F2]. In practice, this means that a report should not only state the score but also explain what the score means, why it is meaningful, and how it compares to chance and other reliability indicators.

## Evidence-based guidance on reporting IAA and selecting the right metric

Reporting inter-annotator agreement requires judgment about what is meaningful, how to handle incomplete data, and how to best express uncertainty. The evidence supports a careful, multi-metric approach rather than relying on a single number.

A higher score can be meaningful when it reflects genuine consistency in labeling, especially if the task is well-specified, the guidelines are clear, and the annotators are trained. However, the evidence warns that raw agreement percentages can be misleading and that high agreement may not always indicate meaningful reliability [N1-F2]. For example, a high observed agreement can be driven by class imbalance or by a majority class rather than by genuine consistency [N1-F2]. Similarly, the evidence on medical image segmentation notes that high inter-annotator agreement supports enhanced clinical decision-making and risk prediction, but also that agreement is important because variability among experts introduces noise into training data [N5-F3]. So the meaning of a higher score depends on context: it is meaningful when it reflects true reliability rather than chance, imbalance, or overly simplistic labeling.

A useful rule of thumb is that a score alone is not enough. The evidence on common statistical methods for assessing rater agreement recommends reporting two or more indicators that should point in the same direction [N1-F1]. This helps avoid over-interpretation of a single number.

## Factors that can affect agreement scores

Interpreting agreement scores requires caution because a number alone does not fully capture the reliability or validity of the annotation process. ### 1) How agreement is measured in different annotation tasks

Agreement is measured differently depending on the task type because the nature of the annotations determines which metric is appropriate. The evidence repeatedly identifies **Cohen’s kappa**, **Fleiss’ kappa**, and **Krippendorff’s alpha** as the main agreement metrics, with some context for continuous or more complex annotations [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]. 

- **Cohen’s kappa** is most commonly used for **categorical labeling** involving two raters [N1-F1][N1-F2]. It is designed for binary or multi-class categorical data and accounts for chance agreement.
- **Fleiss’ kappa** is used when there are **multiple raters** and the outcome is categorical [N1-F1][N5-F3]. It generalizes Cohen’s kappa to more than two raters and is appropriate for tasks where multiple annotators label the same item independently.
- **Krippendorff’s alpha** is used when the task involves **any number of raters** and **any measurement scale**, including nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio data [N1-R2][N1-F2]. The evidence explicitly states that it generalizes to any number of raters, any measurement scale, and missing data [N1-F2].

For **categorical vs ordinal vs continuous annotations**, the evidence explicitly links the measurement scale to the choice of metric. For categorical data, Cohen’s kappa, Fleiss’ kappa, and Krippendorff’s alpha are all appropriate, but they differ in whether they assume a fixed number of raters or more general settings [N1-F1][N1-F2]. For ordinal annotations, the evidence on common statistical methods for assessing rater agreement notes that several methods are used, including variants of the kappa statistic, the agreement coefficient by Gwet, and Krippendorff’s alpha [N1-F1]. This implies that ordinal labels are compatible with these metrics, but the choice may depend on the study design and whether the scale is treated as nominal, ordinal, or continuous.

For **continuous annotations**, the evidence is less direct, but it does suggest that more nuanced measures are needed. The evidence on medical image segmentation reports both Cohen’s Kappa and F1-score to evaluate IAA and also uses heatmaps and STAPLE to quantify and visualize agreement [N5-F3]. It also notes that the task can involve qualitative assessments, such as severity, which are mutually exclusive categories, and that segmentation tasks require careful adaptation of the metric [N5-F3]. In general, the evidence supports the idea that continuous or spatial annotations may require specialized implementations or complementary measures beyond simple categorical kappa.

The evidence shows that implementation details matter greatly in practice. For example:

The evidence further says that F1-score is used alongside Cohen’s Kappa in some settings because it directly reflects overlap between annotated spans [N6-R4]. This shows that span-level NER requires not only a metric but also careful handling of partial overlap and annotation discrepancy.
- **Segmentation**: The evidence on medical image segmentation reports heatmaps, extended Cohen’s kappa, Fleiss’ kappa, and STAPLE [N5-F3]. - **Part-of-speech tagging**: The evidence on POS tagging shows that models sensitive to inter-annotator agreement can perform better on downstream tasks like chunking [N2-R1]. - **Categorical tasks** → Cohen’s kappa, Fleiss’ kappa, Krippendorff’s alpha [N1-F1][N1-F2]

Agreement scores are heavily influenced by the design and execution of the annotation process itself. #### a) How annotation guidelines and instructions shape agreement
Guidelines define what counts as correct and how to resolve boundary cases. When guidelines are vague, annotators may interpret them differently, leading to lower agreement even among careful annotators. The evidence also notes that IAA can reveal task ambiguity, underspecified guidelines, or variation in rater preferences [N3-R1]. This suggests that agreement scores should be viewed as diagnostic tools for guideline quality rather than as standalone quality metrics. In practical terms, a high score with weak guidelines may mask confusion or inconsistent application, while a lower score with well-specified guidelines may indicate a genuinely challenging task.
